tip.title: PIE: Persuade, Inform, Entertain
tip.text: Authors write for a reason. To PERSUADE: convince you to think or do something (ads, letters to the editor, speeches). To INFORM: give facts and explain (textbooks, news, how-to guides). To ENTERTAIN: tell a story or make you feel something (fiction, poems, jokes). Clues: strong opinion words (should, must, best) point to persuade; facts and numbers point to inform; characters and plot point to entertain. A text can mix purposes, so ask which one is strongest.

passage.title: A Letter to the School Paper
passage.text:
Dear Editor,

Every afternoon, the line at the canteen stretches past the flagpole. Students spend half of their twenty-minute break just waiting, and many give up and buy junk food from the gate instead. This is not a small problem. A student who skips a proper meal cannot focus in the afternoon classes, and the teachers notice.

I am proposing that the school open a second serving window during recess. The canteen already has the space; it only needs one more staff member for forty minutes a day. Last year, Mabini High School did exactly this, and their average waiting time fell from eleven minutes to four. Our school could do the same.

Some will say the cost is too high. But think of what we lose now: wasted break time, hungry students, and money going to vendors outside the gate instead of our own canteen. A second window would pay for itself within a semester.

I urge the student council and the principal to try it for one month. If it does not work, close the window. But I am certain it will.

Sincerely,
Andrea Villanueva, Grade 6 Hope

words.meaning: suggesting a plan or idea for others to consider
words.example: The mayor is proposing a new bike lane.

words.meaning: to strongly encourage someone to do something
words.example: Doctors urge people to drink more water.
The first semester ends in October.

items.prompt: What is the author's MAIN purpose?
choices: To entertain readers with a story about the canteen
To inform readers about Mabini High School
To persuade the school to open a second serving window
To describe junk food
items.why: The letter argues for a change and uses words like "I am proposing" and "I urge."

items.prompt: Which sentence is the strongest clue that the author wants to PERSUADE?
choices: "The canteen already has the space."
"I urge the student council and the principal to try it for one month."
"Dear Editor,"
"Last year, Mabini High School did exactly this."
items.why: "I urge" directly asks the reader to act, which is the heart of persuasion.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what happens because the canteen line is so long?
choices: Teachers give the students a longer break.
Many students give up and buy junk food from the gate instead.
The canteen closes early.
Students skip their afternoon classes.
items.why: "Students spend half of their twenty-minute break just waiting, and many give up and buy junk food from the gate instead."

items.prompt: According to the author, why can a student not focus in the afternoon classes?
choices: The classrooms are too hot after lunch.
The student is tired from standing in line.
The student skipped a proper meal.
The teachers are watching the student.
items.why: "A student who skips a proper meal cannot focus in the afternoon classes." The skipped meal is the cause.

items.prompt: Why does the author mention Mabini High School?
choices: To entertain the reader with a story
To give evidence that the plan has worked elsewhere
To complain about another school
To change the topic
items.why: Real results from another school make the proposal more convincing.

items.prompt: What was the effect of Mabini High School opening a second serving window?
choices: The canteen needed ten more staff members.
Students stopped buying from the gate.
The school paper wrote a story about it.
The average waiting time fell from eleven minutes to four.
items.why: "Last year, Mabini High School did exactly this, and their average waiting time fell from eleven minutes to four."

choices: The canteen has space for one more window.
Mabini High School is a better school than ours.
The author proposes a second serving window, which needs little and already worked at Mabini High School.
Last year a school cut its waiting time to four minutes.
items.why: Choice C keeps the proposal, the small cost, and the proof from Mabini. Choices A and D are single details, and choice B is a claim the letter never makes.

items.prompt: Which statement is a FACT the author uses, not an opinion?
choices: "This is not a small problem."
"Their average waiting time fell from eleven minutes to four."
"I am certain it will."
"A second window would pay for itself."
items.why: The waiting-time numbers can be checked. The other choices are the author's beliefs or predictions.

choices: A second window is worth its cost because the school already loses break time, students' meals, and money to outside vendors.
Vendors outside the gate earn a lot of money.
The cost of a second window is too high.
The school will save money within a semester.
items.why: Paragraph 3 answers the cost objection by listing "what we lose now." Choice B is a detail, choice C is the opposing view, and choice D is only the last sentence.

items.prompt: Which is the BEST summary of the whole letter?
choices: Students at the school eat too much junk food.
Andrea wants the canteen to serve healthier food next semester.
Mabini High School has a faster canteen than ours.
Because the long canteen line wastes students' break, the author asks the school to try a second serving window for one month.
items.why: Choice D has the problem, the proposal, and the one-month trial. Choices A and C are single details, and choice B is a request the letter never makes.
